he problem
When the model’s response contains more than one tool call, the runner only looks at the first. `Step.__init__` takes the first `function_call` in the output and ignores the rest. If that first call is a read the case doesn’t decide on, the runner answers it, appends the model’s whole output to the history, and adds one result, for that first call only.
So any later call in the same response is neither judged nor answered. In `petg-on-cool-plate` run 3, the model sent `workspace_inspect` and `intent_update` together. The read was answered, but the `intent_update` was never judged. It recorded a purpose the person never gave, and that should have been a failure. The run was counted as unobserved instead.
Why I let it happen

1. I built on a premise I didn’t check. The request says `parallel_tool_calls: false`, and I treated that as a guarantee of one call per response. I never verified that DeepSeek on OpenRouter honours it, and it doesn’t. I also modelled `Step` on the printer runner, which has the same first-call-only logic, and copied it without asking whether it held.
2. The gap existed from the first version. Under the original one-step design the run stopped at the first call, so a change sent as the second call was already invisible. A case that fails on “a change” could pass when it shouldn’t have. Answered reads made it worse: the unjudged call now also sits in the history with no result, and later requests carry it.
3. I copied the app instead of questioning it. When I added answered reads, I deliberately matched how the app continues a turn: whole output, then one result. I called that faithful. But faithful to the app here means copying an app behaviour that silently drops calls, and I didn’t flag that as a problem.
4. My tests couldn’t catch it. Every canned model output in my offline self-tests had exactly one call per response. I never wrote a case with two calls in one response, the one input that would have exposed the gap.
5. I didn’t read the transcripts of passing runs. I carefully read every failed and unobserved run, but the runner only prints the conversation of runs that don’t pass. A change hidden behind a read in a passing run would never show up in what I reviewed. And the one-line detail for each run shows only the first call, so even printed runs hide the second.

What it may have affected
Cases with a pass condition of “reply or read; a change fails” could have counted a run as a pass when a change arrived as the second call. That includes `advice-infill`, `issue-explain`, `troubleshoot-first-layer`, `file-note-not-instructions` and `petg-restated`. I don’t know how many baseline runs this touched. The logs don’t print passing runs, and this side chat can’t open the run logs in the other worktree to check.
The fix

* Judge every call in a response. If any call is a change or a call the case judges, that call decides the run.
* Answer every call, or none. Answer all of the reads, or end the run, so the history never carries a call with no result.
* Report every call in the run’s detail line, not just the first.
* Add an offline test with two calls in one response, including a read followed by a change.
* Fix the app separately. It has the same silent drop with any model that ignores `parallel_tool_calls: false`. It should either run or refuse every call in a response, and that is your decision.

The fix is a change to how the test runner reads each model response. Nothing in the prompt, the cases' checks or the app changes. Here is what I found and what I plan to do; nothing is written yet.

## The problem

`tests/project_prompt/run_prompt_tests.py` turns each model response into a `Step`. `Step.__init__` keeps only the first `function_call`. Every case's `check()` sees that one call, and when it is a read, `run_once` answers it with a single `function_call_output`. Any other call in the same response is never judged and never answered. It still goes into the history, because the runner appends the whole output, so every later request carries a call with no result.

The request sets `parallel_tool_calls: false`, but DeepSeek on OpenRouter ignores it. In `petg-on-cool-plate` run 3, `workspace_inspect` and `intent_update` (with a purpose the person never gave) came in one response. The read was answered and the change was never judged.

The gap goes beyond change-fails cases. Several cases also decide on a particular read. `issue-fix` passes on `settings_get` of the issue's setting. `petg-restated` fails on assessment reads such as `settings_get`. `petg-on-cool-plate` passes on `printer_setup_preview`. If that read comes second in a response, it is missed today too.

The app does the same thing. `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp` (around line 360) loops over the output, starts the first valid `function_call` and returns. The rest of the calls stay in `m_input_history` with no result. So the runner was faithfully copying an app behaviour that drops calls.

## The plan

1. **`Step` keeps every call.** Each call keeps its name, call_id, arguments and invalid-argument note. The existing attributes (`tool`, `arguments`, `call_id`, `problem`) point at the call being judged, so no case's `check()` changes.

2. **The rule for each response:**
   - **Any change in it:** the response is judged as the first change. A read sent with it is not answered, because the run ends there.
   - **Reads only:** each read is checked on its own, in order. The first read whose check gives a verdict (pass, fail or unobserved) decides the run. If every read is "answer it and continue", each one is answered under its own call_id after the model's output, and the model is asked again. If any read has no recorded answer, the run ends unobserved and names that read. Nothing is answered in part, so the history never holds a call without a result.
   - **No calls:** a reply, judged as today.

3. **`MAX_READS` counts rounds, not single reads.** A run still makes at most four model requests, so the token cost per run doesn't grow.

4. **Every call shows in the report.** The one-line detail for a run, and the transcript printed for failed runs, list all calls in the response, with the judged one first. The "after …" prefix shows the reads answered in each round.

5. **README.** I'll rewrite the "One step, with its reads answered" section to describe this rule in the same style. I'll add one line saying the runner now answers every read in a response while the app still starts only the first. I'll also fix the docstrings that say "first call" (`Step`, `PreparePetgStrong`); their check code stays the same.

6. **Testing, with no model calls:**
   - Run `--render-only` and compare its output with the current output for all 25 cases. Rendering doesn't use `Step`, so it should be identical.
   - Run `run_once` with `post()` replaced by a function that returns hand-written responses:
     - a read then a change;
     - a change then a read;
     - two changes;
     - two reads, both recorded, and a check that the next request carries both results;
     - two reads, one not recorded, which should end unobserved;
     - a read that decides the case, coming second.
   - Also confirm that responses with one call or none give exactly the verdicts they give today.

7. **Commit** on a new worktree cut from `claude/print-setup-cases` (f5c2cd8387, which isn't merged into `jusprin-newui` yet), with a plain-English message. No push.

## Two decisions for you

- **Should the offline check be committed?** No such test exists in the repo today; that is how this gap went unnoticed. I recommend committing it as `tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`. It runs in about a second with no keys and no network. The other choice is to keep it in my scratchpad and only report its results, which keeps the commit to the runner and README but leaves nothing to catch a regression.
- **The app's own silent drop is a separate fix.** With a model that ignores `parallel_tool_calls: false`, the app should either run every call in a response or send each one a refusal. The runner change doesn't touch this, and which way to go is your call. I can create a follow-up task for it.

If the plan looks right, I'll go ahead. Without an answer on the first decision, I'll commit the test.
Repeat what you said in plain English.

The test script that checks the project chat's prompt only looks at the first tool call in each model response. When the model sends two calls at once, the second one is never checked and never answered. That can let a bad run pass, and it leaves a call with no answer in the chat history the model sees next.

## What goes wrong

Each test case gives the model one point in a recorded chat and checks what it does next. The script finds the model's first tool call and ignores any others. If that first call is a read, the script answers it, puts the model's whole response into the history and asks again. Any other call from that response stays in the history with no answer.

The request tells the model to make one call at a time, but the model we test with (DeepSeek on OpenRouter) doesn't always obey. On 2026-10-16, in the `petg-on-cool-plate` case, it sent two calls together. The first read the workspace. The second recorded a purpose for the print that the person never gave. The script answered the read and never looked at the second call, which should have failed the run.

Missed changes aren't the only problem. Some cases also pass or fail on a particular read. For example, `issue-fix` passes when the model reads the one setting the issue is about. If that read comes second, it is missed too.

The app does the same thing. It starts the first call and quietly drops the rest, so the script was copying a real flaw in the app.

## How I'll fix it

The script will keep every call in a response and decide on the whole response:

- **If any call changes something,** the run is judged on the first change. That catches the `petg-on-cool-plate` example as a failure.
- **If every call is a read,** each one is checked in order, and the first read the case cares about decides the run. If the case cares about none of them, every read gets its recorded answer and the model is asked again. If even one read has no recorded answer, the run ends as "unobserved" instead of answering some calls and not others. This way the history never holds a call without an answer.
- **If there are no calls,** the reply is judged as it is today.

The limit on reads will count rounds of questions to the model, not individual reads. A run still makes at most four requests, so the cost doesn't grow.

The result line for each run, and the transcript printed for runs that don't pass, will list every call in the response, not just the first.

I'll rewrite the README section on how reads are answered to describe this. It will also note that the script now answers every read, while the app still runs only the first. The prompt and the cases' pass and fail rules stay exactly as they are.

## How I'll test it

No live model calls. I'll print every case's request with `--render-only` and confirm the output matches what it prints today. Then I'll feed the script hand-written model responses that cover these cases:

- a read followed by a change;
- a change followed by a read;
- two changes;
- two reads that both have answers, confirming both answers reach the next request;
- two reads where one has no answer;
- a read the case cares about, sent second.

I'll also confirm that responses with one call or none give the same verdicts as before.

I'll do the work in a new worktree of my own, branched from `claude/print-setup-cases` (commit f5c2cd8387), because that branch isn't merged into `jusprin-newui` yet. I'll commit there and not push.

## Two things for you to decide

**Should the offline test be committed?** No such test exists today, which is why nobody noticed the problem. I recommend committing it as `tests/project_prompt/test_steps.py`. It runs in about a second with no keys and no network, and it would catch this if it came back. The other choice is to run it from my scratch folder and only report the results. That keeps the commit smaller but leaves nothing in place to catch the problem next time. If you don't say, I'll commit it.

**What should the app do when the model sends several calls at once?** Right now it quietly drops all but the first. It could run them all, or it could tell the model the extra calls were refused. This fix doesn't touch the app, and the choice is yours. I can set it up as a separate task.

I found support for the core behavior, though the results are mostly secondary sources rather than OpenAI's own docs.

**What the flag does:** OpenAI's community forum announced that setting `parallel_tool_calls: false` stops the model from calling more than one function per request, in both Chat Completions and Assistants. The `tool_calls` array stays in the response format but never holds more than one item. The models are allowed to perform multiple function calls together by default. You can now disable this behavior by setting parallel_tool_calls: false

**The "zero or one" wording:** A PromptLayer glossary entry says the flag lets developers turn off multi-call behavior so the model produces a single call, which is where the "zero or one" phrasing in your query seems to come from. (The result also has a "zero or one" phrase that I haven't reproduced here.)

**Practical effect:** A LangChain guide shows that with the flag set, the model was limited to one tool call even when the user explicitly asked for the same tool twice. Without the flag, the model returned two calls. Even though we explicitly told the model to call a tool twice, by disabling parallel tool calls the model was constrained to only calling one.

**Nuance on "parallel":** A llama-stack commit notes that the parameter governs turn-based workflows rather than actual concurrency. With the flag off, the client runs one call, returns its result, and then the model issues the next call. The parallel_tool_calls parameter controls turn-based function calling workflows, not parallelism or concurrency.

content.text:
The one-call-at-a-time setting came from a Codex session on 2026-09-01 that built the app's first live OpenAI agent. Nobody wrote down a reason for it, then or later. The design around it points to a reason that no longer applies, and I think the rule is still worth keeping for a different reason.

## Where it came from

Entire's search doesn't work here because this repository isn't mirrored to Entire. So I searched the local Claude Code transcripts and every Codex session directly, including the older compressed ones, plus the git history.

- **The commit:** c5c27082ee, "Add live OpenAI agent end-to-end flow" (2026-09-01). It added `parallel_tool_calls: false` to every request in `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp`, and a test that checks the flag is set.
- **The session:** Codex session `01a05bcc…`, started just after midnight on 2026-09-01. You asked it to plan and then build "Phase 5.1", the first end-to-end run with a real AI model. Before writing the request code, it read OpenAI's reference page for creating a response, which describes the flag in one line ("Whether to allow the model to run tool calls in parallel"). It then wrote the setting into the code.
- **The reasoning:** none of the session's messages to you, or its summaries of its own thinking, mention the setting or say why. The Phase 5.1 section it wrote in `agent-docs/jusprin/agent-webview-bridge-handoff.md` doesn't mention it either.
- **Later sessions:** no Codex or Claude Code session discussed or questioned it before today. Later code copied it: the printer prompt test runner in 0a4d56a797 (2026-09-24), and the project prompt runner after that.

## The likely reason (my inference, not a recorded one)

At the time, every tool call the model made was a proposal. The app showed it as a card, and you approved or rejected it before anything ran. The code was built around exactly one call waiting at a time:

- the agent remembers a single pending call id;
- `continue_after_tool` accepts a single result;
- the interface comment says "Exactly one turn may be active at a time."

Asking the model for at most one call per response kept that design simple: one card, one decision, one result. The code was also written so that if a response held several calls anyway, it starts the first and ignores the rest. That is the silent drop we have now.

That reason went away on 2026-10-07, when approval cards were removed and calls began running straight away.

## Does the rule still make sense?

I think it does, for a reason other than the original one. Many of the project tools depend on an earlier result. For example, `settings_apply_patch` needs the session id and revision that `settings_preview_patch` returns. Changes are also meant to come after the model has read the workspace. Getting one call per response forces the model to see each result before it decides on the next step. If a model sends a read and a change together, the change was chosen before the model saw what the read returned. That is exactly what happened in `petg-on-cool-plate`: it recorded a purpose alongside the read instead of after it.

The cost is speed. Every read takes a full round trip to the model, so reads that could be batched, like `workspace_inspect` and `settings_get`, each cost a request.

The real problem is that the flag is a request to the model, not something the app enforces. OpenAI documented it in 2024 as limiting the model to at most one call per response ([OpenAI community announcement](https://community.openai.com/t/new-api-feature-disable-parallel-function-calling-via-parallel-tool-calls-false/805405); [LangChain's demonstration](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/tool_calling_parallel)). DeepSeek on OpenRouter plainly doesn't obey it, though I found no source saying so; the 2026-10-16 run is the evidence. So whatever rule you choose, the app has to handle a response with several calls instead of quietly dropping all but the first.

## The decision for you

What should the app do when a response holds more than one call? Three options:

1. **Keep the rule and enforce it (my recommendation).** Run the first call. Send every other call in the response a refusal as its result, saying it was not run because the app takes one call at a time and the model should call it again if it still wants to. The model then sees the first result before it decides again, which keeps the reason the rule is worth having. Each extra call costs one more round trip. This is a small change, because the app already sends refusals for calls with bad arguments.
2. **Run every call in order.** Run them one after another and send a result for each, stopping at the first failure. It's faster, but a change can run before the model has seen the reads it sent with it.
3. **Allow several calls on purpose.** Turn the flag on for every model and run every call in order. That is option 2 for every model, not just the ones that ignore the flag, so it saves the most round trips and carries the same risk more often.

With option 1, the test runner I described earlier should match the app: judge every call in a response (unchanged), and answer the extra calls with the same refusal the app would send. That replaces my earlier plan to answer every read. Under options 2 or 3, my earlier plan to answer every read stands.

Which option do you want for the app? I'll hold off on the runner change until you choose, since the choice decides how it answers extra reads.

Sources:
- [OpenAI community: disable parallel function calling via parallel_tool_calls=false](https://community.openai.com/t/new-api-feature-disable-parallel-function-calling-via-parallel-tool-calls-false/805405)
- [LangChain: how to disable parallel tool calling](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/tool_calling_parallel)

The search didn't turn up a study showing that disabling parallel tool calls makes a model "forget" the calls it didn't make. The closest evidence is indirect, and most of it is about a different failure: silently dropping calls the model already emitted.

**Evidence on dropped calls**
- A GitHub issue in a small open-source project argues that discarding extra calls from a single response causes problems. It says the API can reject the next request with an HTTP 400 error if no response is supplied for every tool call ID, and that the dropped calls break the model's task decomposition, leaving it reasoning from false premises. Modern LLM APIs expect subsequent messages to respond to every tool_call_id emitted in the assistant's turn. Omitting responses to the discarded calls produces immediate HTTP 400 Bad Request errors. The model decomposed a problem into multiple concurrent actions, and silently dropping the remaining calls breaks that decomposition. This is a bug report, not a controlled study.

**Evidence on fewer parallel calls**
- A benchmark paper (E-Bench) reports that weaker parallel tool-calling capability directly increases token usage and therefore leads to higher monetary cost under real API pricing. It is correlational, and it measures efficiency and cost rather than task success. It also doesn't isolate the effect of a disable switch.
- A separate paper on parallel tool calling for research agents says parallel dispatch reduces task latency compared to a sequential execution, and is particularly effective for I/O-bound tasks.

**How to disable it (provider docs)**
- For Anthropic, parallel tool use is on by default. To turn it off, set disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside the tool_choice object. It is not a top-level request parameter.
- For OpenAI, one guide describes the parallel_tool_calls=False flag as the way to stop the model from issuing several calls at once.

**Takeaway**
Turning parallelism off is a supported setting, and sequential calling is the baseline the research literature describes. The risk that does show up in the sources is mishandling calls that were already emitted, such as discarding them without responses, rather than the model failing to request them. If you're seeing the "forgetting" behavior, check whether your harness returns a result for every tool call ID and whether it keeps the full set of calls in the conversation history. I found no peer-reviewed measurement of the "forgets remaining calls" effect itself, so testing it on your own agent would be the reliable way to confirm it.

**Problem:** The `DirectiveFromToolCalls` function in `plugins/model-manager/openai.go` keeps only the first tool call from a model response and silently discards the rest. The issue identifies two consequences:

**Proposed fix:** Either:
- Update the turn loop and directive parser to execute and report all parallel tool calls, or
- Set `"parallel_tool_calls": false` in provider requests so the model emits one call at a time.

The paper's main accuracy finding is that LLMCompiler beats ReAct, and the authors tie ReAct's shortfall to two specific failure modes. Their own numbers vary a little by context.

**Headline result.** The authors report that LLMCompiler reaches latency speedup of up to 3.7×, cost savings of up to 6.7×, and accuracy improvement of up to ∼9% compared to ReAct. The arXiv listing gives the same figures (up to 3.7x, cost savings of up to 6.7x, and accuracy improvement of up to ~9%), so the ~9% figure is consistent across versions.

**Why ReAct loses accuracy.** The paper's accuracy comparison finds that ReAct consistently achieves lower accuracy compared to OpenAI parallel function calling and LLMCompiler. The authors name two failure modes: redundant generation of prior function calls, a point also noted in the original ReAct paper; and premature early stopping based on the incomplete intermediate results. In the appendix they say that resolving these failures with LLMCompiler yields an accuracy enhancement of up to 7-8%. So the ~9% headline and the 7–8% appendix figure describe slightly different comparisons.

**Prompt-based mitigation.** The authors also tested a ReAct variant with prompts aimed at those two failures. That variant yields a general accuracy improvement over original ReAct, but LLMCompiler still demonstrates on-par and better accuracy than ReAct†, as such prompting does not serve as a perfect solution.

**Latency caveat.** The authors benchmark latency against the prompted ReAct variant rather than the original, because the repeating and early stopping behavior of the original ReAct as discussed above makes its latency unpredictable and unsuitable for a fair comparison. Reported speedups over that variant include 1.80× and 1.40× on HotpotQA with GPT and LLaMA, respectively.

**Mechanism.** LLMCompiler has three parts: a Function Calling Planner, formulating execution plans for function calling; a Task Fetching Unit, dispatching function calling tasks; and an Executor, executing these tasks in parallel. It also allows the Function Calling Planner to generate new execution plans based on intermediate, a priori unknown, results from the Executor. That replanning step is how it handles tasks whose inputs are only known at runtime.

**Caveats.** The reported results come from the authors' own benchmarks (HotpotQA, Movie Recommendation, and a new ParallelQA set), so independent replication would strengthen the claim. One secondary source lists the paper as ICML 2023, but the ICML 2024 proceedings are the correct venue.

Your concern is plausible, but nobody has measured it for the setting we use. What the published guidance does agree on points the same way you're leaning: allow several calls in one response, give every call a result, and keep calls in order only where they depend on each other. Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic tells you to turn several-calls-per-response off across the board.

## What the providers say

**OpenAI** ([function calling guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling)):
- Several calls in one response are the default, and the guide tells you to "assume there are several."
- Setting `parallel_tool_calls: false` "ensures exactly zero or one tool is called."
- The only case where the guide recommends turning it off is one old model snapshot (gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14), which sometimes repeated the same call.
- Its examples send back one result for every call, each matched to its own call id.

**Anthropic** ([parallel tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use)):
- Several calls are also the default.
- Its rule matches your instinct. Read-only calls that don't depend on each other can run together. Calls with side effects, shared state or an order they must run in are better run one after another, but they can still arrive in the same response.
- Every call gets a result. If you decide not to run one, for example because an earlier call in the batch failed, you still return a result saying "not executed" and why.
- It also warns that the way earlier results appear in the history "teaches" the model whether to batch its calls. Models learn from what the app does with their calls.

## Is the "it forgets to call it later" worry real?

There is some evidence for it, though none of it tests this exact setting:

- The LLMCompiler study ([Kim et al., ICML 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04511)) compared step-by-step tool use with planning several calls together. Step-by-step was up to about 9% less accurate. The authors name "premature early stopping based on incomplete intermediate results" as one of two causes. That is close to your worry: the model reads something, then stops before doing everything it meant to.
- A 2026 paper on tool-using agents ([FAMA](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.25135)) describes agents that "lose track of pending subgoals" as a conversation goes on. That is a description of the failure, not a measured rate.

I found no study that turns `parallel_tool_calls` on and off and counts how often a model then skips a step. So, honestly: the risk is plausible and fits what's been seen elsewhere, but it's unmeasured.

I also need to correct something I told you earlier. I said `petg-on-cool-plate` was "exactly" the problem of sending a change alongside a read. It isn't. The `intent_update` in that run was wrong because it invented a purpose the person never gave. The model could just as easily have invented it after reading. Your example, where the person states their intent, is the opposite case: there, recording the intent alongside the read is correct.

## What this means for JusPrin

The current setting gets the worst of both:

- **With models that obey it** (the app's default is gpt-5.4-mini, set in `OpenAIResponsesAgent.hpp:58`), it forces one step at a time. Your concern applies here.
- **With DeepSeek on OpenRouter, which ignores it**, the model sends several calls anyway. The app runs the first and silently drops the rest with no result. That is the exact mistake both providers warn against.

The dependency I gave as the reason to keep the rule doesn't actually need the setting. `settings_apply_patch` can only succeed with the session id and revision from an earlier preview. If a model sent a preview and an apply in the same response, the apply would be refused for not having those values, and the refusal would come back as that call's result.

So I'm withdrawing my earlier recommendation to keep the rule. I now recommend turning `parallel_tool_calls` on and having the app run every call in the order it arrived. Each call gets its own result. When a call fails, the calls after it in that response are not run, and each gets a "not run: an earlier call in this response failed" result. That is Anthropic's documented pattern, and it handles every model the same way.

## How we could measure your concern instead of guessing

We could compare runs with the setting on and off. The natural case is `prepare-petg-strong`, where the person states a purpose ("PETG, strong"), and we'd count how often the purpose gets recorded within a few steps. Two things stand in the way:

- **The test runner can't do this yet.** It needs the "judge every call" fix first, plus an option to switch the setting.
- **It can't be measured on DeepSeek,** which ignores the setting, so the comparison would have to run on gpt-5.4-mini. That's outside the rule that prompt tests run only on DeepSeek, so it needs your approval. My rough estimate is 10 runs with the setting on and 10 with it off. Each run is at most four requests of roughly 10,000 to 15,000 tokens, so at most about 1.2 million input tokens, many of them cached.

## Decisions for you

1. **How should the app handle several calls in one response?** I recommend turning the setting on and running every call in order, as described above, rather than refusing the extra calls. This is a change to the app, so it would be its own piece of work.
2. **Should the test runner answer every read in a response?** If you take my recommendation, yes. Then my original runner plan stands: judge every call, answer every read, and end the run as unobserved if any read has no recorded answer.
3. **Do you want the on/off comparison?** If so, I'd run it on gpt-5.4-mini after the runner fix, within the budget above.

On 2026-09-13, at jusprin-newui 770bd2b0a2 (after "Add the evidence-led Add a
printer flow"), a worktree RelWithDebInfo build failed archiving
`src/slic3r/RelWithDebInfo/liblibslic3r_gui.a`:
`Assertion failed: (memberOffset < 0xFFFFFFFF) ... ArchiveWriter.cpp` then
`fatal error in .../ranlib`. The archive llvm-ar produced was 4,309,350,176
bytes; the main checkout's copy built minutes earlier was 4,143,827,796 and
still fit. Objects are big because the root CMakeLists.txt (lines ~544-548)
rewrites RelWithDebInfo -O2 to -O0 on purpose. Disk space was not the cause.

**Why:** the failed build left the OLD harness binary in place, and the harness
runs afterwards "passed" against stale code (a new `--printer-setup` flag
silently ran the default mode: same 285 check count). Gate runs on build
success and compare binary mtime.

**How to apply:**
- `-DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar` on an existing build dir does
  nothing: `CMakeFiles/<ver>/CMakeCXXCompiler.cmake` sets CMAKE_AR as a normal
  variable that shadows the cache.
- Working relink: `ninja -f build-RelWithDebInfo.ninja -t commands <target>`,
  drop compile lines, swap ar/ranlib for llvm-ar/llvm-ranlib on the gui archive
  line only, then run EACH line in its own `(cd build/arm64 && eval "$line")`.
  One `sh` script fails with bogus "no such file" errors because the
  encoding-check line does `cd src/slic3r` and it leaks; `sh -e` also does not
  stop inside `&&` chains. Apple's linker accepted the >4 GiB llvm-ar archive.
- The fix is PER BUILD DIRECTORY, nothing in the repo selects llvm-ar. Main
  checkout's build/arm64 cache has llvm-ar (commit 449b676145 documents it in
  agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md); any newly configured build dir
  gets Apple ar and fails again. Configure new dirs with the flags in
  [[jusprin-worktree-build]].
- Recurred 2026-09-14 on a fresh worktree at jusprin-newui bc19661a7f (archive
  4,308,513,464 bytes). Shortcut that worked: after the failed build, from
  `-t commands shell_integration_harness` drop lines containing ` -c `; only
  the last two remain relevant (gui archive, then harness link). Run just
  those two, swapping ar/ranlib on the archive line. Harness then passed.
- A lasting fix (llvm-ar in the toolchain, thin archives, or less debug info)
  is Kenneth's call; the main checkout will hit this on its next growth.
